name: Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
summary: The oculomotor nerve carries motor fibers from the oculomotor nucleus to four of the six extraocular muscles (medial, superior and inferior recti, inferior oblique) and the levator palpebrae, and parasympathetic fibers from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus to the ciliary ganglion for the pupil and lens. It leaves the midbrain into the interpeduncular fossa between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, runs beside the posterior communicating artery and the uncus, enters the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus and passes through the superior orbital fissure. Because the pupillary fibers lie on its surface, compression (aneurysm, herniation) involves the pupil early while microvascular ischemia of the core spares it, the single most important distinction in third nerve palsies.

anatomy.location: Nucleus in the periaqueductal gray at the superior colliculus → fascicles through the red nucleus and medial crus → interpeduncular cistern lateral to the PComm and medial to the uncus → roof then lateral wall of the cavernous sinus (uppermost nerve) → superior orbital fissure within the annulus of Zinn, dividing into superior (levator, superior rectus) and inferior (medial and inferior recti, inferior oblique, parasympathetic root to the ciliary ganglion) divisions.

function: Elevation, depression and adduction of the eye, elevation of the upper lid, pupillary constriction and accommodation.

bestView.label: nerves emerging in the interpeduncular fossa between PCA and SCA
third nerve in the roof and lateral wall of the cavernous sinus
oculomotor nuclear complex in the ventral periaqueductal gray

imaging.normalAppearance: The cisternal nerve is a fine line on thin T2 (CISS) between the PCA above and the SCA below, passing close to the PComm; enhancement of the nerve is abnormal (inflammation, lymphoma, sarcoid). CTA is mandatory when the pupil is involved. The HCP1065 mesh in this atlas shows the cisternal course.

pathology.finding: Saccular aneurysm at the ICA–PComm junction compressing the nerve; subarachnoid blood if ruptured.
Normal imaging; pupil-sparing palsy in a patient with vascular risk factors that recovers in weeks to months.
Medial temporal lobe through the tentorial notch compressing the nerve.
Paramedian midbrain restriction involving the fascicles.
Mass or thrombosis involving III with IV, V1, V2 and VI.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CTA or MRA immediately for pupil-involving palsies; MRI with contrast for nuclear, fascicular and cavernous lesions

lesionEffects.deficit: Ptosis, eye down and out, diplopia
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of levator and of all recti except lateral; unopposed lateral rectus and superior oblique

lesionEffects.deficit: Dilated, unreactive pupil with loss of accommodation
lesionEffects.mechanism: Parasympathetic fibers on the nerve surface (compressive lesions)
Ischemia of the nerve core (diabetes, hypertension)

lesionEffects.deficit: Bilateral ptosis and contralateral superior rectus weakness
Aberrant regeneration: lid elevation on down-gaze, pupil constriction on adduction
lesionEffects.mechanism: Misdirected regrowth after compressive injury, never after ischemia

examination: Ductions in all directions; note the resting position
Pupil size and reaction to light and near
Ask about pain (aneurysm and ischemia both hurt; pain does not discriminate)
Examine IV, V1, V2 and VI for cavernous sinus involvement and the contralateral limbs for midbrain signs
pearls: A complete third nerve palsy with a normal pupil in a diabetic is ischemic; any pupil involvement or partial palsy needs urgent vascular imaging
A dilated pupil alone without ptosis or ophthalmoplegia is almost never a third nerve palsy: think Adie, pharmacological or trauma to the iris

pitfalls: Myasthenia gravis mimics a pupil-sparing third nerve palsy with fatigable ptosis; the pupil is always normal in myasthenia

nuclei.component: GSE to extraocular muscles and levator; GVE (Edinger–Westphal) to the ciliary ganglion

exit.brainstemExit: Medial surface of the cerebral peduncle in the interpeduncular fossa
exit.cisternalCourse: Between the PCA and SCA, lateral to the PComm, medial to the uncus and the tentorial edge, to the roof of the cavernous sinus
exit.foramen: Superior orbital fissure (within the annulus of Zinn)
exit.extracranialCourse: Superior division to levator and superior rectus; inferior division to medial and inferior recti, inferior oblique and the ciliary ganglion

branches.name: Inferior division
branches.supplies: medial rectus, inferior rectus, inferior oblique; parasympathetic root to the ciliary ganglion

reflexes.name: Pupillary light reflex (efferent)
reflexes.efferent: oculomotor nerve → ciliary ganglion → sphincter pupillae

reflexes.name: Accommodation
reflexes.center: cortex → Edinger–Westphal and medial rectus subnuclei
reflexes.efferent: oculomotor nerve to ciliary muscle, sphincter and medial recti

tests.name: Ductions and versions
tests.how: Follow a target in an H pattern; ask about diplopia in each direction
tests.abnormal: Limited elevation, depression and adduction; eye rests down and out

tests.name: Lid
tests.how: Measure palpebral fissure and levator excursion

tests.name: Pupil
tests.how: Compare size in light and dark; test light and near reactions
tests.abnormal: Dilated, poorly reactive pupil on the affected side

tests.name: Cover test
tests.how: Cover-uncover in primary and other positions

lesionSigns.localisingValue: compression: PComm aneurysm, uncal herniation, tumor; imaging today

lesionSigns.sign: Palsy with contralateral hemiparesis, ataxia or tremor
Palsy with IV, VI and V1 signs
lesionSigns.localisingValue: cavernous sinus or superior orbital fissure
orbital apex or fissure (though nuclear and fascicular lesions can mimic)

cranial.nuclearVsPeripheral: Nuclear lesions differ from nerve lesions in two ways set by the wiring of the complex: the levator is supplied by a single midline caudal nucleus, so nuclear lesions cause bilateral ptosis, and each superior rectus subnucleus supplies the opposite eye, so a nuclear lesion weakens elevation of the contralateral eye. Fascicular lesions in the midbrain add contralateral signs from the red nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle or crus.
cranial.supranuclear: Conjugate gaze commands reach the nucleus through the MLF (horizontal, from the contralateral abducens nucleus) and the riMLF and posterior commissure (vertical). A supranuclear gaze palsy spares the vestibulo-ocular reflex and never causes ptosis, pupil change or diplopia, which separates it from a nuclear or nerve lesion.
